This vignette gives methods and results text to adapt, a guide to which
number to take from which file, and short answers to questions reviewers
often ask. The reasoning behind each answer, with the simulations, is in
`vignette("rationale", package = "RADdiversity")`; the analysis itself is in
`vignette("workflow", package = "RADdiversity")`. Simulation figures quoted
below can be re-run with the script or function named in the rationale's
Appendix C.

## Methods text to adapt

Replace the bracketed parts with what you did. Keep only the sentences that
apply.

> Loci were assembled with Stacks [version] and exported with `populations`
> [settings, e.g. requiring genotypes to be supported by ≥ 6 reads
> (`--min-gt-depth 6`) and each locus to be genotyped in ≥ 80% of individuals
> within each population (`-r 0.8 -p 2`)]. [No minor-allele-count filter was
> applied to the data used for diversity statistics. / Sites with a minor
> allele count below [X] were removed; this removes rare alleles and lowers
> per-site diversity and allelic richness, so these values are comparable only
> with data filtered the same way.] [No Hardy-Weinberg filter was applied,
> because a heterozygote deficit is the quantity under study.]
>
> Diversity statistics were computed with RADdiversity [version] in R
> [version]. Expected heterozygosity was estimated with the estimator of Nei &
> Chesser (1983), which is unbiased when individuals are inbred, and F<sub>IS</sub>
> as 1 − ΣH<sub>o</sub>/ΣH<sub>e</sub> summed over loci. H<sub>o</sub> and
> H<sub>e</sub> were computed from the SNP VCF and are also reported per
> sequenced site (Schmidt et al. 2021); F<sub>IS</sub> and allelic richness
> were computed from the haplotype VCF, with allelic and private allelic
> richness rarefied to [g] gene copies (Kalinowski 2004). Standard errors
> [and 95% confidence intervals] were obtained by [a delete-one-locus
> jackknife / a bootstrap over RAD loci], so that linked SNPs were resampled
> together. [Because individuals differed in inbreeding (identity
> disequilibrium g2 = [value], 95% CI [..]; David et al. 2007), standard
> errors from a delete-one-individual jackknife are also reported.]
>
> Heterozygosity was compared between populations with Welch's *t*-test on
> per-individual heterozygosity, so that individuals rather than loci were the
> unit of replication (Van Dongen 1995), with a Wilcoxon rank-sum test as a
> distribution-free check [and a Welch one-way ANOVA across all
> populations, followed by pairwise tests with Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted
> p-values]. [Differentiation was measured as F<sub>ST</sub> (Weir &
> Cockerham 1984) and Jost's D (Jost 2008); the global D was computed from
> the [D_records] loci genotyped in every population, and each pairwise D
> from the loci genotyped in both populations of the pair.] Differences in
> inbreeding were tested in the same way on individual inbreeding
> coefficients. [Individuals were screened for close
> relatives with KING-robust (Manichaikul et al. 2010), and one individual of
> each pair with kinship above 0.0442 was removed.]

## Results

For each comparison give the difference, its 95% confidence interval, the
test statistic or p-value, and Hedges' *g*. If the test is not significant,
write **"no difference in heterozygosity was detected (Welch's t = …, p = …,
95% CI of the difference … to …)"**, not "the populations do not differ".
Power comes from the number of individuals: with 15 and 10 individuals,
Welch's test detects a moderate difference (half a standard deviation of
individual F) less than 20% of the time and a large one (0.8 SD) about 40% of
the time, so say how many individuals the comparison rests on.

## Which number to take from where

| statistic | file | source | note |
|---|---|---|---|
| H<sub>o</sub> | SNP VCF | `diversity_stats()` or Stacks `Obs_Het` | the same observed proportion; Stacks also averages sites with a single genotyped individual, which `diversity_stats()` skips (`min_n`), so values can differ slightly |
| H<sub>e</sub> per variant site | SNP VCF | `diversity_stats()`, or Stacks `Pi` (Variant positions) | differ by about F/(2N − 1), usually < 1% |
| H<sub>e</sub> per sequenced site (π) | SNP VCF | `diversity_stats(sites = )`, `pi_allsites()`, or Stacks `Pi` (All positions) | the values to compare with other studies |
| % polymorphic | SNP VCF | `diversity_stats()` | report next to per-variant H<sub>e</sub> |
| F<sub>IS</sub> | haplotype VCF | `diversity_stats()` | not Stacks' `Fis` (see below) |
| allelic richness, private allelic richness | haplotype VCF | `diversity_stats()` | Stacks' `Private` is an unrarefied count |

Label every table with the file its numbers came from: H<sub>o</sub> and
H<sub>e</sub> from the haplotype VCF are per RAD locus and are much larger
than per-SNP values, so a reader checking 1 − H<sub>o</sub>/H<sub>e</sub>
across files would find a discrepancy. F<sub>IS</sub>, a ratio, is
comparable between files.

If you take some numbers from Stacks and some from RADdiversity, say so, and
use `estimator_comparison` from `diversity_stats()` to state how much the two
H<sub>e</sub> estimators differ in your data.

## Null alleles and allele dropout

Mutations in restriction sites make some chromosomes produce no reads, so
heterozygotes look homozygous (or go missing). This inflates F<sub>IS</sub>
and cannot be removed by depth filtering. It is also more common in more
diverse populations (Gautier et al. 2013), so it can make F<sub>IS</sub>
differ between populations, and it can understate a real difference in
H<sub>e</sub>. Report `fis_by_call_rate` from `diversity_stats()`: if
F<sub>IS</sub> rises as call rate falls, show F<sub>IS</sub> from well-typed
loci too. A sentence to adapt:

> Allele dropout at restriction-site polymorphisms can inflate F<sub>IS</sub>
> in RAD data (Gautier et al. 2013). F<sub>IS</sub> did [not] increase among
> loci with lower call rates [and was similar when estimated from loci
> genotyped in all individuals (F<sub>IS</sub> = …)].

---

## If a reviewer asks

**"SNPs within a RAD locus are linked; you should use one SNP per locus."**

> They are linked, which is why standard errors and confidence intervals were
> obtained by resampling whole RAD loci, so linked SNPs move together.
> Thinning is then unnecessary and loses information: in simulations with a
> known F<sub>IS</sub> of 0.10, one SNP per locus gave an unbiased estimate
> but a wider 95% interval (0.035) than all SNPs (0.031) or haplotypes
> (0.028).

**"Why doesn't your F<sub>IS</sub> match the value Stacks reports?"**

> Stacks averages per-site F<sub>IS</sub> values, counting sites monomorphic
> in a population as zero, and each per-site value divides by `Pi`, which
> assumes F<sub>IS</sub> = 0. We used the ratio of sums over loci
> (1 − ΣH<sub>o</sub>/ΣH<sub>e</sub>) with Nei & Chesser's H<sub>e</sub>, as
> in Weir & Cockerham (1984) and hierfstat. Stacks' own columns do not
> reconcile for the same reason: its `Fis` column differs from
> 1 − `Obs_Het`/`Pi` computed from the same file.

**"Your H<sub>e</sub> does not match Stacks' `Exp_Het`."**

> `Exp_Het` is the uncorrected 1 − Σp<sup>2</sup>, which is biased low in small
> samples: Stacks' `Pi` = `Exp_Het` × 2N/(2N − 1), 3.4% higher at N = 15. The
> comparable Stacks column is `Pi`,
> which differs from our estimate only by about F/(2N − 1), because our
> estimator does not assume F<sub>IS</sub> = 0.

**"Why not simply use Stacks' π?"**

> Stacks' `Pi` is fine as an estimate of diversity: its bias, F/(2N − 1), is
> usually under 1%. F<sub>IS</sub> divides by that quantity, so the same bias
> becomes a larger relative error in F<sub>IS</sub> (roughly 3–5% at
> N = 10–15), and it depends on sample size, so it does not cancel between
> populations of different size.

**"Why is H<sub>e</sub> from the SNP data but F<sub>IS</sub> from the haplotype data?"**

> Haplotype gene diversity has no fixed upper limit: a locus with more SNPs
> can carry more haplotypes, so its value depends on read length, enzyme and
> SNP calling. In simulations, varying only the number of SNPs per locus
> changed haplotype H<sub>e</sub> by 66% and per-SNP H<sub>e</sub> by 24%.
> F<sub>IS</sub> is a ratio, so that scale cancels, and haplotype loci
> estimate it more precisely. The ratio of H<sub>e</sub> between populations
> was the same from both files.

**"Why per variant site rather than per sequenced site?"** (or the reverse)

> Both are reported. Per-variant-site values allow comparison with earlier
> studies of this system; per-sequenced-site values are the ones comparable
> across studies (Schmidt et al. 2021).

**"Your H<sub>e</sub> is averaged over sites where the population is monomorphic, which deflates it."**

> That is deliberate: both populations are scored over the same sites.
> Averaging each population only over its own polymorphic sites discards the
> sites where it lost variation, which is part of its lower diversity; in
> simulation of a bottlenecked population this reversed the direction of a
> real difference in diversity. The percentage of polymorphic sites is
> reported alongside, and the pooled value equals the within-population value
> times that percentage, so either can be recovered.

**"How much of your data went into these numbers?"**

> A locus was used for a population once that population had at least
> [min_n] genotyped individuals there, decided separately for each
> population; [N of M] loci met this in [population]. [Alternatively: only
> loci genotyped in every individual were used (Schmidt et al. 2021,
> recommendation (b)); [N of M] loci.] Per-site values were scaled by each
> population's own count of sequenced and variant sites.

**"An allelic richness near 2 is uninformative."**

> Richness was computed from the haplotype data, where a RAD locus is one
> multi-allelic marker; on biallelic SNPs rarefied richness cannot exceed 2.

**"Why not report Stacks' private allele counts?"**

> Stacks' `Private` column is a raw count, which grows with sample size and
> cannot be compared between populations of different size. We report
> private allelic richness rarefied to a common number of gene copies
> (Kalinowski 2004; Szpiech et al. 2008).

**"Schmidt et al. (2021) recommend calling SNPs separately for each population."**

> We followed their recommendation to report heterozygosity per sequenced
> site [and their recommendation to use only loci typed in every individual,
> as a sensitivity analysis]. We called SNPs jointly so that both populations
> were scored on the same set of loci under the same rules; separate runs can
> call different variant sets in each population, and the per-site scaling
> used each population's own count of sequenced sites.

**"You should have filtered loci for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium."**

> A heterozygote deficit is the quantity under study, so an HWE filter would
> remove the signal measured by F<sub>IS</sub>. Filtering on HWE also affects
> inferences of population structure (Pearman et al. 2022). Departures from
> Hardy-Weinberg proportions were tested and are reported [in Table S…].

**"Why a t-test on individuals rather than a bootstrap over loci?"**

> Loci are repeated measurements on the same individuals, not independent
> replicates of a population mean. In simulations of two populations with
> identical heterozygosity, a bootstrap over loci rejected the null about half
> the time when individuals differed moderately in inbreeding (SD of F = 0.10)
> and about 80% of the time when they differed more, against a nominal 5%;
> Welch's t on per-individual heterozygosity stayed near 5% (Van Dongen 1995
> made the same point). The overdispersion of individual heterozygosity in our
> data was [X], meaning a locus-based test would have understated the
> standard error about [√X]-fold.

**"Your confidence intervals resample loci, but individuals vary."**

> We tested whether individuals differ in inbreeding (g2 = [value], 95% CI
> [..]; David et al. 2007). [If the interval excluded 0:] We therefore report
> standard errors from a delete-one-individual jackknife, which in simulation
> kept 93–95% coverage where locus-based intervals fell to 28–66%. [If it
> included 0:] Locus-based intervals are appropriate in that case; in
> simulation they kept about 95% coverage when individuals did not differ.

(If you report individual standard errors for allelic or private allelic
richness, note that in simulation the one for private richness ran up to
about 20% small, and both ran large when many loci had barely *g* gene
copies; see `vignette("rationale")`, section 4.)

**"A non-significant result may just reflect low power."**

> We agree, and report it as no difference detected. With [n1] and [n2]
> individuals, simulation shows limited power for moderate differences, so the
> confidence interval of the difference is the more informative result.

**"RAD data have null alleles; your F<sub>IS</sub> may be inflated."**

> We checked for this: allele dropout makes F<sub>IS</sub> rise among loci with
> more missing data (Gautier et al. 2013), and F<sub>IS</sub> [did not / did]
> [rise with falling call rate; when estimated from loci typed in all
> individuals it was …].

## References

David, P., Pujol, B., Viard, F., Castella, V. & Goudet, J. (2007) Reliable
selfing rate estimates from imperfect population genetic data. *Molecular
Ecology* 16:2474–2487.

Gautier, M., Gharbi, K., Cezard, T., et al. (2013) The effect of RAD allele
dropout on the estimation of genetic variation within and between
populations. *Molecular Ecology* 22:3165–3178.

Jost, L. (2008) G<sub>ST</sub> and its relatives do not measure
differentiation. *Molecular Ecology* 17:4015–4026.

Kalinowski, S.T. (2004) Counting alleles with rarefaction: private alleles
and hierarchical sampling designs. *Conservation Genetics* 5:539–543.

Manichaikul, A., Mychaleckyj, J.C., Rich, S.S., Daly, K., Sale, M. & Chen,
W.-M. (2010) Robust relationship inference in genome-wide association
studies. *Bioinformatics* 26:2867–2873.

Nei, M. & Chesser, R.K. (1983) Estimation of fixation indices and gene
diversities. *Annals of Human Genetics* 47:253–259.

Pearman, W.S., Urban, L. & Alexander, A. (2022) Commonly used Hardy–Weinberg
equilibrium filtering schemes impact population structure inferences using
RADseq data. *Molecular Ecology Resources* 22:2599–2613.

Schmidt, T.L., Jasper, M.-E., Weeks, A.R. & Hoffmann, A.A. (2021) Unbiased
population heterozygosity estimates from genome-wide sequence data.
*Methods in Ecology and Evolution* 12:1888–1898.

Szpiech, Z.A., Jakobsson, M. & Rosenberg, N.A. (2008) ADZE: a rarefaction
approach for counting alleles private to combinations of populations.
*Bioinformatics* 24:2498–2504.

Van Dongen, S. (1995) How should we bootstrap allozyme data? *Heredity*
74:445–447.

Weir, B.S. & Cockerham, C.C. (1984) Estimating F-statistics for the analysis
of population structure. *Evolution* 38:1358–1370.
